name: Drospirenone

lead: Drospirenone is a prescription progestin in some contraceptive pills. In the pill Yaz it is labelled in the US for moderate acne in women at least 14 who also choose the pill for contraception. Women use these pills for clearer skin, and the fluid retention seen with some older progestins is reduced.

It blocks androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors as well as activating the progesterone receptor, which lowers androgen signalling in skin and so oil production. Its antiandrogenic action is the usual explanation for the acne benefit.

paras: It is taken by mouth, most often as a combined pill with an estrogen on a daily schedule set by a prescriber. Skin changes with hormonal pills are generally judged over a few months.

Common effects include headache, irregular bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness and mood changes. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35, and registry studies have reported more venous clots with drospirenone pills than with levonorgestrel pills, though the size of the difference is debated. Rarely it can raise potassium. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Drospirenone blocks androgen receptors, which reduces sebum production and leads to clearer skin. It is prescribed to women in contraceptive pills, and the FDA labels certain drospirenone pills for moderate acne in women who also want contraception.

lead: Drospirenone is a synthetic progestin, structurally related to the diuretic spironolactone, that is taken by mouth in birth-control pills and in menopausal hormone therapy. Besides activating the progesterone receptor it blocks the androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors, a profile that is often described as closer to natural progesterone than that of older progestins.[1][2] The antiandrogenic part of that profile is why people interested in clearer skin, less oiliness and, in some conditions, less excess hair growth encounter it.[1][3]

For appearance, its best-documented role is acne. A US-labelled combination of drospirenone with a low dose of ethinyl estradiol (Yaz) is indicated to treat moderate acne in women aged 14 and over who also want an oral contraceptive, and the labelled trials showed larger lesion-count reductions than placebo over six cycles.[4] A Cochrane review of combined oral contraceptives for acne found that the drospirenone pills were favoured for clinician-assessed clear or almost clear skin.[5] Its antimineralocorticoid action counters the water retention that estrogens can cause, and some users choose it for that reason.[1][6]

Drospirenone pills carry the same boxed warning about smoking and cardiovascular events as other combined oral contraceptives, and large registry studies and a network meta-analysis have examined whether drospirenone-containing pills are associated with more venous thromboembolism than levonorgestrel pills.[4][7][8][9] It is prescription-only in the US, Canada and Australia, and is marketed under brand names including Yasmin, Yaz, Slynd, Nextstellis and Angeliq.[1]
infobox: Moderate acne in women 14 and over who want an oral contraceptive (Yaz)[4]
Yasmin, Yaz, Slynd, Nextstellis, Angeliq; generics such as Ocella, Gianvi[1]

paras: Drospirenone combined with ethinyl estradiol has an FDA-labelled indication for moderate acne in women aged 14 and over who choose an oral contraceptive for birth control.[4] The acne indication is tied to use as a contraceptive: the label limits it to patients who want contraception, so it is not an acne-only treatment.[4] Wikipedia lists acne, premenstrual syndrome, premenstrual dysphoric disorder and painful menstruation among indications for the low-dose ethinylestradiol pills, and attributes the acne benefit to drospirenone's antiandrogenic activity.[1][2]

Dermatology reviews group combined oral contraceptives with spironolactone, cyproterone acetate and topical clascoterone as hormonal options for acne, and drospirenone-based pills are one of the COC choices within that group.[10] Reviews of treatments for hirsutism and of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) likewise place COCs among anti-androgen approaches to excess hair growth and acne.[3][11]

A small 2026 retrospective cohort of 60 overweight or obese women with PCOS compared a drospirenone-only pill with a cyclic progestin; the drospirenone group had lower testosterone and free androgen index and lower modified Ferriman-Gallwey hirsutism scores at 3 and 6 months.[12] A 2026 randomised trial in PCOS compared estetrol/drospirenone with a drospirenone-only pill and reported lower hirsutism scores with the estetrol combination.[13]

Drospirenone's antimineralocorticoid action counters the sodium and water retention that estrogens can promote, and Wikipedia reports that it maintains or slightly reduces body weight in studies.[1][6] Forum users have long discussed whether Yasmin-type pills cause less bloating than older pills; one 2003 T Nation post described the then-new formula as supposed to be better in this regard.[14]

Drospirenone is used for contraception in combined pills (with ethinyl estradiol or estetrol) and in a progestogen-only pill (Slynd, approved in the US in 2019), and for menopausal hormone therapy together with estradiol (Angeliq, approved 2005).[1] It has also been used as a component of hormone therapy for transgender women.[1] The Yaz label also lists premenstrual dysphoric disorder; in a primary trial of 384 evaluable women, scores improved by an average of 37.5 points on drospirenone versus 30.0 with placebo.[4]

The Yaz label describes two multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in 889 subjects aged 14 to 45 with moderate acne, who took the pill or placebo for six 28-day cycles. Inflammatory lesions fell by about 48 and 51 per cent with the pill versus 32 and 34 per cent with placebo; total lesions fell by 42 and 46 per cent versus 25 and 31 per cent; and 15 and 21 per cent of drospirenone users were rated clear or almost clear versus 4 and 9 per cent with placebo.[4]

A 2012 Cochrane review of combined oral contraceptives for acne covered 31 trials and 12,579 participants. It found that several COCs, including levonorgestrel, norgestimate and dienogest combinations, reduced total lesion counts against placebo, and that drospirenone was favoured for clinician-assessed clear or almost clear skin (odds ratio 3.02, 95% confidence interval 1.99 to 4.59).[5] The authors' conclusions were unchanged from earlier versions, which had found that COCs reduce facial acne lesions.[5]

A 2026 analysis of reporting databases using ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone as the reference found that drospirenone-containing pills were associated with higher reported rates of acne, migraine, depression and anxiety; such database reports describe what users reported and are distinct from placebo-controlled trial results.[15] Wikipedia lists acne among the reported adverse effects of drospirenone-only use (3.8 per cent of women).[1]

The US label for drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol reports headache or migraine, menstrual irregularities, nausea or vomiting, breast pain and mood changes as the most frequent adverse reactions in contraception and acne trials.[4] For the drospirenone-only pill, Wikipedia reports unscheduled bleeding in roughly 40 to 64 per cent of women, with acne, headache, breast pain, weight gain and decreased libido each reported in a few per cent.[1]

Because drospirenone has antimineralocorticoid effects, potassium can rise. Hyperkalemia is uncommon: it led to discontinuation in about 0.2 per cent of women taking the drospirenone-only pill, and potassium monitoring is advised for women with kidney disease or who take other potassium-raising drugs.[1] Contraindications include renal impairment, adrenal insufficiency, hyperkalemia, liver tumours or impairment and undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding.[1]

The label carries a boxed warning that cigarette smoking raises the risk of serious cardiovascular events with combined oral contraceptives, particularly in women over 35, and states that such women should not use the product.[4]

Combined pills containing ethinyl estradiol raise the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) compared with non-use. Wikipedia gives an absolute risk of about 3 to 10 per 10,000 women per year on such pills versus 1 to 5 in non-users.[1] Whether drospirenone differs from older progestins has been examined in several studies. The Dutch MEGA case-control study reported odds ratios versus non-users of 3.6 for levonorgestrel pills and 6.3 for drospirenone pills, and the Danish national cohorts also reported higher VTE rates with drospirenone-containing pills than with levonorgestrel pills; a network meta-analysis compared many pill types.[7][8][9][16][16]

The FDA label states that drospirenone combined pills may be associated with a higher VTE risk than levonorgestrel-containing ones, with studies ranging from no increase to about a threefold increase, and advises weighing this before starting them.[4] A large European active surveillance study of a drospirenone-containing pill covering 142,475 woman-years reported its own safety findings.[17] Wikipedia notes the relative-risk estimates (roughly 1.3 to 2.0 times levonorgestrel in some studies) are debated because of possible confounding, and some prospective and case-control studies found no difference.[1] Danish data have also examined stroke and myocardial infarction with hormonal contraception.[18]

A 2026 systematic review of estetrol/drospirenone pills (25 publications) reported smaller haemostatic effects than with ethinyl estradiol comparators while rating the certainty of evidence on thromboembolic risk as very low.[19]

Bayer, the maker of Yasmin and Yaz, faced thousands of US lawsuits over blood clots and other events. Wikipedia reports more than 12,000 suits by July 2012, with 1,977 cases settled for US$402.6 million at that point, and by July 2015 roughly 10,000 claims settled without an admission of liability and VTE claims totalling about US$1.97 billion, plus a separate US$56.9 million settlement for arterial events.[1]

Drospirenone acts as an agonist of the progesterone receptor and an antagonist of the androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors, without estrogenic activity; it suppresses ovulation.[1][4][20] Its antimineralocorticoid action counters sodium and water retention that estrogens can promote, which is why it is described as less likely to cause bloating-type effects than some other progestins.[1][6] Reviews of progestin pharmacology classify it among agents with antiandrogenic properties.[21]

According to Wikipedia, its antiandrogenic activity is greater than that of spironolactone but about 30 per cent of cyproterone acetate's in animals. Unlike more androgenic progestins it does not blunt the effect of ethinylestradiol on sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and lipids, which is one explanation offered for its antiandrogenic profile in pills.[1]

Per Wikipedia, oral bioavailability is roughly 66 to 85 percent, protein binding about 95 to 97 percent and elimination half-life about 25 to 33 hours, with metabolism largely independent of cytochrome P450 enzymes though CYP3A4 inhibitors can raise levels.[1] A 2000 review characterised its pharmacokinetics in detail.[20]

Drospirenone is a synthetic steroidal 17-alpha-spirolactone (1,2-dihydrospirorenone). Compared with spironolactone it lacks the 7-alpha acetylthio group and has additional methylene bridges, and removal of that group appears to restore progestogenic activity.[1]

Drospirenone was synthesised and patented in 1976 by Schering AG, including chemist Rudolf Wiechert, as a spironolactone-derived progestin.[2] It was first marketed in 2000 in a pill with ethinylestradiol (Yasmin in Europe), and the US FDA approved Yasmin in 2001; Yaz, a lower-dose 24/4 regimen, followed in 2006.[1][2] Estradiol/drospirenone (Angeliq) for menopausal therapy was approved in 2005, a progestogen-only pill in 2019 and an estetrol combination in 2021.[1] Wikipedia calls it a 'fourth-generation' progestin because of its introduction date.[1]

Brand names include Yasmin, Yaz, Slynd (Slinda in some regions), Nextstellis and Angeliq; generics are widely available.[1] It is prescription-only in the US, Canada and Australia, and in 2023 the drospirenone/ethinylestradiol pill was among the 200 most-prescribed drugs in the US with more than 3 million prescriptions.[1][22]

Public discussion of drospirenone pills outside medical literature centres on skin, bloating and mood. One 2006 T Nation forum post claimed that Yasmin enlarged breast size and said this had been mentioned in the news, an effect not described in the US label.[23][4] Pharmacovigilance analyses report mood and skin-related reports among users, and the legal history of the product is dominated by the clot litigation.[15][1]

Contraceptive efficacy has been studied in large trials, for example a 13-cycle Phase 3 study of a drospirenone-only pill in about 1,550 participants and a US study of the Yaz pill in 1,027 women that reported a Pearl Index of 1.41.[24][4] The acne trials (889 subjects) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder trials are described in the labelling, and the Cochrane review pooled acne trials of combined pills.[4][5]

Registered current trials include drospirenone-only pill pharmacokinetics after bariatric surgery, estetrol/drospirenone in endometriomas, and use of drospirenone in adenomyosis.[25][26][27] Safety has been examined in the cohort and case-control studies described above.[7][8][9][17]

lore.intro: Drospirenone appears in pill-focused discussion more than in looksmaxxing-specific threads: forum posts about it concern bloating and body shape, while the skin question is mostly addressed in clinical sources.[14][23]
